opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've gone back and forth on. The worry with asking a forecasting model a direct question, something like "Will X happen by 2030?", is that the question itself carries information. Just by choosing to ask about X, you're signaling that X is salient and plausible enough to be worth asking about. A model trained on human text has absorbed the pattern that questions people bother to ask tend to be about live possibilities. So you can end up measuring your own framing rather than the model's actual beliefs about the world.

Open-ended generation is appealing because it avoids that. Instead of asking about a specific event, you condition the model on, say, a plausible document from the future, like a news article or an encyclopedia entry dated a few years out, and let it write. Then you look at what it fills in. If it spontaneously writes about some development you never prompted it about, that's arguably a cleaner signal of what it thinks is likely.

But I'd say it's not a free lunch, for a few reasons. First, the framing problem doesn't disappear, it just moves. Choosing which kind of document to condition on, what date, what publication, is still a choice, and it still shapes the output. A future article from a tech blog will look very different from one in a policy journal.

Second, open-ended text is optimized for being a plausible-looking document, not a calibrated forecast. Models tend to produce stories that are narratively typical. They regress toward stereotyped futures and the kinds of things that get written about, rather than reflecting the actual probability of mundane or surprising outcomes. Things that are likely but boring may simply not show up.

Third, it's hard to evaluate. With a direct question you get a probability you can score once the outcome is known. With open-ended text you have to do a lot of interpretation afterward: extract claims, decide what counts as a prediction, aggregate over many samples. That interpretation step can introduce its own biases.

So my view is that it's a useful complement. You can sample a lot of open-ended futures to discover which possibilities the model considers salient, things you might not have thought to ask about. Then you can turn those into more structured questions and check whether the model's direct answers line up with the frequency at which those things appear in its free-form generations. If they disagree, that tells you something interesting, either about the framing effects or about inconsistency in the model itself. Using both and looking for agreement seems a lot more robust than trusting either method alone.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended generation can reduce question-framing bias, but it does not state that normalizing over all possible newspaper headlines provides that protection.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss likelihood-based comparisons between forecasting models or predicted writing style dominating those comparisons.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair bit, and I want to be careful here because I think it's one of those ideas that sounds more clean than it actually is in practice.

So the motivation is pretty intuitive. If you're trying to use a model to forecast — say, what AI capabilities look like in five years, or how some policy plays out — the moment you pose a specific question, you've already smuggled in a huge amount of framing. You've decided which variables matter. You've decided what counts as an answer. And a lot of the interesting stuff about the future is precisely the things you didn't think to ask about. So the appeal of open-ended generation is: just let the model tell a story. Have it write the history textbook from 2040, or the news article, or whatever, and see what shows up unprompted.

And I do think there's something real there. When you let a model free-generate, you sometimes get it mentioning considerations that would never have occurred to you as the question-asker. That's genuinely valuable as a kind of brainstorming or hypothesis-generation step. It's a way to find out what's in the model's "world model" that you weren't probing for.

But I'd push back on the idea that it avoids bias. I think it just moves the bias somewhere less visible. A few reasons.

One is that open-ended generation is incredibly sensitive to genre. If you ask for a news article, you get news-article-shaped futures — dramatic, event-driven, probably somewhat sensationalist, because that's what news articles are. If you ask for an academic retrospective, you get a sober, tidy narrative with clear causes. Neither of those is a calibrated forecast; they're both the model doing an excellent impression of a text type. And the text type itself is a massive prior on what kind of future you get back. So you haven't removed the question — you've replaced it with a style, and style is arguably an even stronger constraint because it's harder to see.

The second thing is that free text doesn't give you probabilities. If the model writes a plausible story where X happens, I don't know whether that's a 5% world or a 60% world. Narratives are optimized for coherence, and coherence is almost anti-correlated with probability — the more detailed and satisfying a story is, the more conjunctions it's stacking up, so the less likely it is. That's just the conjunction fallacy, but models fall into it beautifully because they've been trained on text that rewards being compelling, not being well-calibrated. So you end up with something that's really persuasive and really uninformative about likelihoods.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that the model has a strong attractor toward "the kind of future people write about." The training data is full of science fiction, think-pieces, forecasting blogs. So when you let it go free, it doesn't give you an unbiased sample from its beliefs — it gives you something that sounds like what's already been written. In a way that's worse than a pointed question, because a pointed question can at least force it off the well-trodden path.

So where I've landed is that I think of open-ended generation as a discovery tool, not an assessment tool. The workflow I'd actually defend is something like: generate a bunch of unconstrained futures, use them to surface variables and scenarios you hadn't considered, and then go back and ask the model very specific, resolvable questions about those things — ideally ones where you can check calibration against something. The open-ended step widens your question set; the structured step is where the actual forecasting happens.

The thing I'd really want to avoid is someone reading a well-written AI-generated future, finding it compelling, and treating that as evidence. Because compellingness is exactly what these systems are best at, and it's basically orthogonal to whether the thing is true.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended generation shifts bias into genre or style, but does not mention normalizing over all possible newspaper headlines as protection against question bias.

r002.rationale: The response describes genre as a strong constraint and says narratives do not provide probabilities, but does not state that writing-style differences can dominate likelihood-based comparisons between forecasting models.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps with one part of the problem. If you ask, “Will there be a war next year?” you’ve already decided that war is the thing worth forecasting. Whereas if you ask a model to continue a news article from next year, you give it some room to bring up things you wouldn’t have thought to ask about.

But you haven’t removed the framing. You’ve still chosen the prompt, the genre, and perhaps which newspaper it’s supposed to be writing for. And a plausible news article isn’t necessarily a representative sample of what might happen. News selects for surprising, noteworthy events; lots of important things don’t look like news at all.

So I’d distinguish using open-ended generation to discover possibilities from using it to assign probabilities. It seems useful for expanding the set of things you’re considering. But I wouldn’t automatically interpret how often something appears in generated text as the model’s probability that it will happen. That connection is something you’d need to test.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended article generation can broaden possibilities, but notes that the prompt and genre still frame the output. It does not state that normalizing over all possible newspaper headlines protects against question bias.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss likelihood-based comparisons between models or predicted writing-style differences dominating those comparisons.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps, but it doesn’t make the problem go away. If you ask, “Will there be a war next year?” you’ve already decided that war is the thing worth forecasting. If you instead ask the model to describe what happens next, it has more freedom to bring up things you didn’t think to ask about.

But there’s still a choice of prompt, and there’s still the question of which kinds of text the model has learned to produce. A plausible news story isn’t necessarily a representative sample of the future. It might favour things that are dramatic or easy to describe.

So I’d distinguish letting the model suggest possibilities from getting calibrated probabilities for those possibilities. Open-ended generation seems useful for the first. It doesn’t, by itself, solve the second.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended prompting gives the model more freedom, but does not mention normalizing over all possible newspaper headlines or state that this protects against question-induced bias.
